claims.text: A low weight fraction of graphene nanoplatelets can be incorporated into a CoCrFeNi matrix during synthesis.
Graphene addition will produce a well-dispersed graphene network in CoCrFeNi.
The graphene network will form a durable and continuous in-situ tribofilm during sliding from room temperature to 800 °C.
Graphene nanoplatelets align under sliding stress to create a low-shear-strength interface.
The proposed graphene tribofilm reduces direct metal-to-metal contact.
The proposed graphene tribofilm mitigates oxidation of the sliding interface.
The proposed graphene tribofilm mitigates plastic deformation during sliding.
Graphene-doped CoCrFeNi will have significantly lower steady-state friction than unmodified CoCrFeNi throughout room temperature to 800 °C.
Graphene-doped CoCrFeNi will have significantly lower wear rates than unmodified CoCrFeNi throughout room temperature to 800 °C.
The starting CoCrFeNi matrix has a homogeneous microstructure.
Unmodified CoCrFeNi struggles to maintain low friction and wear over the full room-temperature-to-800 °C range.
The graphene intervention remains beneficial under variable loads and dry or controlled environmental exposures up to 800 °C.
Extreme loads may eliminate the beneficial effect of graphene addition.
Aggressively oxidizing or chemically reactive environments may eliminate the beneficial effect by attacking graphene.
The beneficial effect may not persist above 800 °C.
Tribological effectiveness may differ between inert and oxidative atmospheres.
Incorporated solid lubricants can improve wear behavior and reduce coefficient of friction in HEA composites.
SEM and EDS can determine the thickness and continuity of the proposed tribofilm.

contradictions.description: The intervention and experiment require an 'optimized' graphene content, while the uncertainty field states that the optimum content remains to be determined; the experiment contains no optimization stage that resolves this.
